items.abstract: Agentic AI systems have proved great capabilities in autonomous task execution. But their deployment in high-stakes domains is still constrained by some basic challenges related to reliability. These are hallucination-induced failures, unverified plan correctness, and brittle coordination mechanisms. In this paper we introduce a new framework ARTEMIS (Adaptive Reliable Task Execution with Multi-agent Intelligence and Self-verification). It’s a multi-agent framework which integrates formal verification, runtime hallucination detection, and adaptive orchestration to achieve provable reliability guarantees. ARTEMIS is based on a three-tier architecture: (1) the first tier is a Formal Planning Layer. This tier generates executionplans which we can verify with mathematical correctness proofs, (2) second tier is a Cross-Agent Verification Module. This module detects and recovers from hallucinations through consensus-based validation, and (3) third tier is an Adaptive Orchestration Engine. This engine dynamically adjusts coordination strategies based on runtime performance metrics. We describe the reliability problem as a constrained optimization over multi-agent execution traces. We then show that ARTEMIS limits error propagation within a fixed bound under certain conditionsWe conduct extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets: TravelPlanner, WebShop, and a new SafetyBench dataset. The results show that ARTEMIS achieves a 94.3% task success rate and 97.8% accuracy in detecting hallucinations. It works out better than the available structures such as AutoGen, LangGraph and Alpha Berkeley. It is also superior to those by 23 to 41% in reliability. Concurrently it is keeping the same latency. Ablution studies are showing that every element of the system is important for improving the reliability. Particularly the verification module alone reduces critical failures by 68%. In whole, this work gives a new approach for building reliable agent-based AI systems with formal guarantees of reliability.
title: ARTEMIS: Adaptive Reliable Task Execution with Multi-agent Intelligence and Self-verification

Introduction 1.1 Background on Agentic AI Any move towards larger agent-based AI systems has been contributed to due to large language models (LLMs) which have good reasoning abilities. These systems are autonomous similar to agents. These are capable of decomposing multi-faceted tasks, using third-party tools, and multi-step processes [1], [2], [3]. They have performed well in most fields such as web navigation [4], software development [5], scientific workflows [6] and enterprise knowledge management [7]. Recent systems such as AutoGen [8], LangGraph [9] and Alpha Berkeley [1] give the simple schemata of management of a number of agents. These structures can enable planning tasks, the use of tools, and communication with human beings better. Even thoughthese improvements are done, agent-based AI systems are not being used at big scale in safety-critical and high-risk environments because of issues related to reliability. Current systems show three main types of failures: (1) Hallucination errors: In this LLMs produce information that seems correct but it is actually wrong. This is error and it spreads through the system [10], [11]; (2) Unverified plans: Here the generated plans are not checked to ensure that they are correct or they meet all constraints [12], [13]; and (3) Weak coordination: In this the fixed control strategies cannot adjust to failures or changes during execution [14], [15]. 1.2 Problem Statement The main problem in making reliable agentic AI systems is described as follows: Let’s say we are given a complex task Tand it has certain constraints, a set of agents with capabilities, and a stochastic execution environment, design a multi-agent system that: 1.Generates an execution plan that provably satisfies all constraints in
2. Detects and recovers from hallucinations during execution with probability $$\:\ge\:1-ϵ$$
3. Adapts orchestration strategies to minimize expected task failure rate under environmental uncertainty

4. Will Provide a formal bounds on error propagation across the agent interactions The frameworks which are available handles only some of the needs. Also they do not provide a complete solution. AutoGen [8] supports flexible multi-agent communication but it does not include formal verification. Alpha Berkeley [1] support human approval, but it has a problem that, it depends on manual checking rather than automatic verification. Agent Q [4] uses Monte Carlo Tree Search for planning but it doesn’t have a perfect way to detect hallucinations. Some latest studies on information sharing [2] and self-organizing networks [16] have improved the coordination, but they still do not guarantee the reliability. 1.3 Research Gap We analysed 30 recent papers (2022–2026) on agent-based AI systems and we found five key research gaps: 1.Absence of formal verification: No existing framework provides mathematical proofs of plan correctness or constraint satisfaction before execution 2.Limited hallucination handling: Current approaches rely on post-hoc detection or human oversight rather than systematic runtime verification 3.Static orchestration: Existing orchestrators use fixed coordination strategies that cannot adapt to execution failures or performance degradation 4.Weak reliability guarantees: Systems lack formal bounds on error propagation, making them unsuitable for safety-critical applications

5. Insufficient robustness evaluation: Most papers report success rates on narrow benchmarks without comprehensive failure analysis or adversarial testing 1.4 Contributions In this paper we present ARTEMIS. It’sa new multi-agent framework for addressing the above gaps. This is done by combining formal verification, real-time hallucination detection, and adaptive coordination. The key contributions of this paper are: Novel Architecture: A three-tier architecture integrating formal planning, cross-agent verification, and adaptive orchestration with provable reliability properties Formal Verification Layer: A constraint satisfaction framework that generates execution plans with mathematical correctness proofs using temporal logic specifications Hallucination Detection Module: A consensus-based verification mechanism that detects LLM hallucinations through cross-agent validation with 97.8% accuracy Adaptive Orchestration Engine: A reinforcement learning-based orchestrator that dynamically adjusts coordination strategies based on runtime performance metrics Theoretical Guarantees: Formal proofs of bounded error propagation and probabilistic reliability guarantees under specified conditions Comprehensive Evaluation: Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrating 23–41% improvement in reliability metrics over state-of-the-art frameworks Robustness Analysis: Systematic failure case analysis, adversarial testing, and ablation studies validating each architectural component The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 is about literature survey and it tells where ARTEMIS stands in the current landscape. Section 3 describes the proposed method, it includes the system design, mathematical model, and algorithms. Section 4 describes the experimental setup and evaluation metrics. Section 5 discusses the results and comparison with other methods. Sections 6 and 7 discuss ablation studies and robustness analysis. Section 8 is about the conclusion of the paper and it suggests future work. 2. Literature Review 2.1 Multi-Agent Orchestration Frameworks Since 2022, multi-agent LLM systems have been developing rapidly and a few key LLM frameworks have emerged which define how agents are organised. AutoGen [8] presented flexible multi-agent conversations based on a conversational programming model where agents communicate with a series of dialogic steps to resolve complex problems. However, it does not have any formal verification and relies on emergent coordination with no clear guarantees of reliability. LangGraph [9] combined a graph-based approach with good state management, where agent workflows are represented as conditional directed graphs. This provides better visibility into the control flow, but has fixed orchestration strategies that are unable to cope with failures during execution. Recent research has focused on developing systems that are ready-to-use in the real world, from researching and developing building systems. Alpha Berkeley [1] Enhances the scalability and human supervision by employing dynamic capability classification, human-approved planning, and production-level execution environments. It has been applied at the Advanced Light Source particle accelerator with the results demonstrating the feasibility of applying agent-based systems in high-risk environments. However, it relies on formal validation through manual human approbation instead of the automatic verification needed for swift performance of time-critical tasks. AegisFlow [17] and AgentOrchestra [18] both propose hierarchical multi-agent designs for general task solving, but these do not offer formal reliability guarantees or a concrete way of detecting hallucination. 2.2 Planning and Reasoning in Agentic Systems Reliable task planning remains a major challenge for agent-based Artificial Intelligence systems. Agent Q [4] is based on agent Q [3], which is a combination of guided Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and self-critique methods that achieved 95.4% success rate on tasks on real world booking. 2Q further achieved through repeated fine-tuning using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). While this has a strong practical performance, it does not show formally if plans are correct and does not give theoretical guarantees on errors. OctoTools [19] shows a framework with flexible tools for dealing with complex reasoning problems but (mainly) focuses on integrating tools rather than on checking whether the generated plans are correct. Recent research on the subject of multi-agent planning has focused on how to enhance the way in which agents share information and coordinate. Ou et al. [2] demonstrate that the use of structured information sharing via a persistent notebook leads to an 18% reduction of hallucination errors in long planning tasks. Further improving the performance by 13.5% are added orchestrator agent. Their work on the TravelPlanner benchmark illustrates the value of reflective coordination however their methods lack formal verification and adaptability. GradientSys [20] uses ReAct-based orchestration to manage multiple agents, however, it does not offer reliability guarantees or any method to detect hallucinations. 2.3 Hallucination Detection and Mitigation Hallucination - when LLMs generate information that seems right, but it is wrong, is a big issue with agent-based systems. Current methods to reduce the problem of hallucinations fall into three main types:(1) post-hoc detection, where outputs are checked against external knowledge bases after they are generated [21]; (2) self consistency checking, in which a number of outputs are produced and compared to select the most consistent one [22]; and (3) human-in-the-loop validation, the human's check and monitors the results [1]. However, these methods have major drawbacks. Post-hoc detection adds delay and requires massive knowledge databases, self-consistency methods take more computation and don't guarantee reliability, and human verification will slow down the process of automated activities by causing bottlenecks. Recent research has been done investigating verification between multiple agents. GraphCogent [23], dealing with the limited working memory of LLMs, using multi-agent collaboration for graph tasks, of an agent working together can overcome the limits of one model. MAS² [24] is a proposal for multi-agent systems that can generate, configure and correct themselves, but that does not incorporate any clear methods for the detection of hallucinations or formal verification. In general, there remains a gap between the practical means of diminishing hallucinations and having formal guarantees of reliability in current research. 2.4 Formal Verification and Reliability Formal verification techniques embraced from software engineering and control theory are not commonly applied in agent-based AI systems. Traditional methods for verifying multi-agent systems use model checking and temporal logic [25] but this assumes that the agents will behave in the same way, that they can for even a long time and that the randomness present in LLM outputs is taken into account. Recent studies about the issue of LLM reliability explore probabilistic verification [26] and measurement of uncertainty [27], but they have not been integrated into whole agent-based systems yet. TB-CSPN [28] presents a turing complete language where the separation of a semantics processing and a logics of coordination is introduced with the support of rule-based control aimed at a greater reliability. However, it limits the usage of LLMs which leads to a decreased flexibility and adaptibility. AgentGit [29] adapts the version control idea to multi-agent systems that use LLMs in which rollback and reproducibility are possible. However, it lacks formal verification of plans and guarantees for reliability in their execution. 2.5 Adaptive and Self-Improving Systems Adaptive orchestration is an emerging field of research. The Self-Organizing Agent Network [16] proposes agent networks created dynamically according to the task, but no clear methods for adaptation and reliability analysis are given. AIME [30] is focused on constructing fully autonomous multi-agent systems that are able to improve themselves, but does not specify how to achieve adaptive orchestration and provide formal guarantees of reliability. The use of reinforcement learning to adaptive coordination has been the study of a few cases. Agent Q [4] uses DPO for repeated fine-tuning which demonstrates that learning from both successful and failed attempts aids in improving performance. However, this approach is focused on the external improvement of individual agents rather than the overall coordination approach. Designing orchestrators that are capable of changing the way agents collaborate as a function of the performance at run-time remains an open problem. 2.6 Comparative Analysis and Limitations Table 1 outlines the advantages and disadvantages of the major frameworks in our review. The analysis reveals that none of the existing frameworks satisfactorily integrate formal verification, hallucination detection, and adaptive coordination with guarantees on reliability. While LangGraph and AutoGen provide loose coordination, they do not offer any verification. Alpha Berkeley incorporates some human oversight, but relies on approvals. Agent Q exhibits strong practical performance but lacks guarantees. Recent advances in self-organizing networks [16] and information sharing [2] have enhanced coordination, but do not offer any concrete bounds on reliability.
